questions.question: The Georgian Period (1910–1936) spans the reign of King George V, who ascended the British throne in May 1910 upon the death of which monarch?
questions.explanation: King Edward VII died on 6 May 1910 and was succeeded by his son King George V who reigned until January 1936.

questions.question: Which two landmark royal events occurred in Britain during the year 1936, marking the close of the Georgian Period?
options: The Silver Jubilee of Edward VII and the outbreak of World War II
The death of Queen Victoria and the coronation of Edward VII
The marriage of George V and the signing of the Anglo-Irish Treaty
The death of King George V and the abdication of King Edward VIII
questions.explanation: In 1936 the Year of Three Kings George V died in January and Edward VIII abdicated in December to marry Wallis Simpson.

questions.question: How many volumes of the anthology series 'Georgian Poetry' were published between 1912 and 1922 under the editorship of Edward Marsh?
questions.explanation: Edward Marsh edited five volumes of Georgian Poetry published in 1912 1915 1917 1919 and 1922.

questions.question: Which famous London bookshop, opened by Harold Monro in Devonshire Street in 1913, published all five volumes of 'Georgian Poetry'?
questions.explanation: Harold Monro founded the Poetry Bookshop in Bloomsbury as a meeting place and publishing house for Georgian and modern poets.

questions.question: Which nostalgic 1912 poem by Rupert Brooke, written at a Berlin café, concludes 'Stands the Church clock at ten to three? / And is there honey still for tea?'
questions.explanation: Written in May 1912 at the Café des Westens in Berlin The Old Vicarage Grantchester became a classic of Georgian pastoral nostalgia.

questions.question: On which Greek island in the Aegean Sea was Rupert Brooke buried in April 1915 after dying of sepsis en route to the Gallipoli campaign?
questions.explanation: Sub-Lieutenant Rupert Brooke died on a French hospital ship on 23 April 1915 and was buried in an olive grove on Skyros.

questions.question: Which Welsh Georgian poet and former tramp wrote the famous couplet 'What is this life if, full of care, / We have no time to stand and stare' in his 1911 poem 'Leisure'?
questions.explanation: William Henry Davies published his famous lyric Leisure in his 1911 collection Songs of Joy and Others.

questions.question: Which classic 1908 prose memoir by W. H. Davies, prefaced by George Bernard Shaw, recounts his life as a transient hobo in America and Britain?
options: Down and Out in Paris and London
questions.explanation: Shaw provided the title and preface for W H Davies 1908 book The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp.

questions.question: Which Georgian poet, famous for 'Salt-Water Ballads' and 'Reynard the Fox', was appointed Poet Laureate in 1930 upon the death of Robert Bridges?
questions.explanation: John Masefield succeeded Robert Bridges as Poet Laureate in May 1930 and held the office until his death in 1967.

questions.question: Which celebrated maritime lyric by John Masefield opens with the line 'I must go down to the seas again, to the lonely sea and the sky'?
questions.explanation: First published in Salt-Water Ballads in 1902 Sea-Fever remained one of the most popular lyrics throughout the Georgian era.

questions.question: Which three-stanza poem by John Masefield contrasts an ancient 'Quinquireme of Nineveh' and a Spanish galleon with a 'Dirty British coaster with a salt-caked smoke stack'?
questions.explanation: Masefield three-stanza unrhymed lyric Cargoes contrasts romantic ancient and Renaissance shipping with modern industrial trade.

questions.question: Which 1913 collection of rhymes and lyrics by Walter de la Mare, containing poems such as 'Silver' and 'Someone', established his fame in imaginative verse?
questions.explanation: Walter de la Mare published Peacock Pie A Book of Rhymes in 1913 blending childhood wonder with eerie twilight atmosphere.

questions.question: In which Gloucestershire village did Lascelles Abercrombie, Wilfrid Gibson, John Drinkwater, Rupert Brooke, Edward Thomas, and Robert Frost form a famous pre-war poetic circle?
questions.explanation: Known as the Dymock Poets the group gathered around the village of Dymock in Gloucestershire between 1911 and 1914.

questions.question: Which American poet lived in Gloucestershire in 1914 and encouraged the literary critic Edward Thomas to begin writing poetry?
questions.explanation: During their daily country walks in 1914 Robert Frost urged Edward Thomas to turn the prose of In Pursuit of Spring into verse.

questions.question: Which Georgian poet and diplomat authored 'The Golden Journey to Samarkand' (1913) and the posthumously staged Oriental verse drama 'Hassan' (1922)?
questions.explanation: James Elroy Flecker died of tuberculosis in Switzerland in 1915 and his lush play Hassan triumphed in London in 1923 with music by Delius.

questions.question: Which Georgian poet won the Polignac Prize in 1914 for his visionary poems 'The Bull' and 'The Song of Honour'?
questions.explanation: Ralph Hodgson printed his poems in penny chapbooks with Lovat Fraser at the Sign of the Flying Fame and collected them in Poems 1917.

questions.question: Which 1918 historical chronicle play by the Georgian poet John Drinkwater brought international acclaim to the Birmingham Repertory Theatre?
questions.explanation: John Drinkwater play Abraham Lincoln premiered at the Birmingham Repertory Theatre in October 1918 and ran for a year at the Lyric Theatre Hammersmith.

questions.question: With what bitter anti-war question does Wilfred Owen's 1917 sonnet 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' begin?
options: What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
Red lips are not so red / As the stained stones kissed by the English dead
Move him into the sun— / Gently its touch awoke him once
questions.explanation: Drafted at Craiglockhart in September 1917 with revisions suggested by Siegfried Sassoon Anthem for Doomed Youth opens with this famous line.

questions.question: In Wilfred Owen's visionary poem 'Strange Meeting' (1918), where do the British narrator and the dead enemy soldier ('I am the enemy you killed, my friend') meet?
options: In a ruined French cathedral in Picardy
Aboard a hospital ship crossing the English Channel
Inside a flooded medical tent at Ypres
Down a profound dull tunnel in Hell
questions.explanation: The speaker imagines escaping out of battle down some profound dull tunnel where he realizes that he is in Hell.

questions.question: On 4 November 1918, exactly one week before the Armistice, while leading his men across which French canal was Wilfred Owen killed in action?
questions.explanation: Second Lieutenant Wilfred Owen of the Manchester Regiment was shot and killed at Ors while crossing the Sambre-Oise Canal on 4 November 1918.

questions.question: Which 1918 collection of searing trench poems by Siegfried Sassoon includes 'The General', 'Base Details', and 'Suicide in the Trenches'?
questions.explanation: Published in July 1918 Counter-Attack and Other Poems established Sassoon harsh satirical realism against the Home Front and military high command.

questions.question: Which working-class painter-poet, killed on the Western Front in April 1918, composed 'Break of Day in the Trenches', featuring a 'queer sardonic rat' and a poppy?
questions.explanation: Born to Jewish immigrant parents and raised in London East End Isaac Rosenberg wrote Break of Day in the Trenches in June 1916.

questions.question: Which Georgian pastoral poet survived Passchendaele and the Somme to publish the classic 1928 prose memoir 'Undertones of War'?
questions.explanation: Edmund Blunden published Undertones of War in 1928 concluding with a supplement of his war verses.

questions.question: Which deeply moving 1933 autobiography by Vera Brittain chronicles her wartime service as a VAD nurse and the loss of her fiancé Roland Leighton and her brother?
questions.explanation: Vera Brittain published Testament of Youth in 1933 speaking for an entire generation of women bereaved by the First World War.

questions.question: Who is the possessive solicitor and art collector—dubbed the 'man of property'—at the center of John Galsworthy's 'The Forsyte Saga' (collected 1922)?
questions.explanation: Soames Forsyte possessive obsession with his first wife Irene drives the central conflict of The Forsyte Saga and its sequel A Modern Comedy.

questions.question: In which year was the English novelist and dramatist John Galsworthy awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.explanation: John Galsworthy was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in November 1932 just two months before his death in January 1933.

questions.question: By what collective regional name are the Staffordshire pottery towns known in Arnold Bennett's realist novels such as 'Clayhanger' (1910)?
questions.explanation: Arnold Bennett renamed the six Staffordshire Potteries towns as the Five Towns Turnhill Bursley Hanbridge Knype and Longshaw.

questions.question: Which 1910 comic realist novel by H. G. Wells follows a dyspeptic bicycle-shop owner who escapes his miserable marriage to find peace at the Potwell Inn?
questions.explanation: Published in April 1910 The History of Mr Polly portrays Alfred Polly burning down his shop in Fishbourne and defeating Uncle Jim at the Potwell Inn.

questions.question: Which unassuming, umbrella-carrying Roman Catholic priest-detective did G. K. Chesterton introduce in his 1911 collection 'The Innocence of Father Brown'?
questions.explanation: Modeled on Father John O Connor of Bradford Father Brown solves crimes through intuitive moral and psychological insight.

questions.question: Which 1915 semi-autobiographical novel by W. Somerset Maugham traces the club-footed orphan Philip Carey through medical school and his obsessive love for Mildred?
questions.explanation: Taking its title from Part IV of Spinoza Ethics Maugham 1915 masterpiece Of Human Bondage chronicles Philip Carey search for meaning.

questions.question: Which 1919 novel by W. Somerset Maugham, inspired by the life of Paul Gauguin, depicts the London stockbroker Charles Strickland abandoning his family to paint in Tahiti?
questions.explanation: Maugham published The Moon and Sixpence in 1919 contrasting bourgeois convention the sixpence with artistic obsession the moon.

questions.question: Under the pen name 'Saki', which satirist—killed in action at Beaumont-Hamel in 1916—authored macabre stories such as 'The Open Window' and 'Sredni Vashtar'?
questions.explanation: Born in Burma Hector Hugh Munro took the pen name Saki from the cup-bearer in the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám.

questions.question: Which supremely resourceful gentleman's personal gentleman did P. G. Wodehouse introduce in 1915 to rescue Bertie Wooster from constant predicaments?
questions.explanation: Reginald Jeeves made his first appearance in the 1915 short story Extricating Young Gussie and took full charge of Bertie Wooster in 1916.

questions.question: In which 1920 debut detective novel did Agatha Christie first introduce her retired Belgian police officer Hercule Poirot?
questions.explanation: Written while Christie worked in a wartime hospital dispensary The Mysterious Affair at Styles was published in 1920 introducing Poirot and Hastings.

questions.question: Which aristocratic amateur detective did Dorothy L. Sayers introduce in her 1923 novel 'Whose Body?' and later pair with the mystery writer Harriet Vane?
questions.explanation: Lord Peter Death Bredon Wimsey assisted by his valet Bunter starred in eleven novels by Dorothy L Sayers between 1923 and 1937.

questions.question: With what famous sentence does the unreliable American narrator John Dowell begin Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel 'The Good Soldier'?
options: The past is a foreign country
This is the saddest story I have ever heard
There was no possibility of taking a walk that day
questions.explanation: John Dowell opens The Good Soldier with This is the saddest story I have ever heard before recounting the infidelity of his wife Florence and Captain Edward Ashburnham.

questions.question: Who is the traditionalist Yorkshire gentleman and government statistician at the center of Ford Madox Ford's four-novel World War I sequence 'Parade's End' (1924–1928)?
questions.explanation: Christopher Tietjens of Groby endures the betrayal of his unfaithful wife Sylvia and the horrors of the Western Front before finding love with Valentine Wannop.

questions.question: In D. H. Lawrence's 'Women in Love' (1920), which two emancipated sisters enter contrasting relationships with the school inspector Rupert Birkin and the mine owner Gerald Crich?
questions.explanation: Continuing the family saga of The Rainbow 1915 Women in Love pairs the teacher Ursula Brangwen with Birkin and the sculptor Gudrun with Gerald Crich.

questions.question: Which controversial 1928 novel by D. H. Lawrence, privately printed in Florence, depicts the affair between an aristocratic wife and her husband's gamekeeper, Oliver Mellors?
questions.explanation: Printed in Florence by Pino Orioli in 1928 Lady Chatterley Lover remained banned in unexpurgated form in Britain until the Penguin trial of 1960.

questions.question: On which island in the Scottish Hebrides is the Ramsay family's summer home set in Virginia Woolf's 1927 novel 'To the Lighthouse'?
questions.explanation: Although inspired by Talland House at St Ives in Cornwall Woolf set the Ramsay holiday home on the Isle of Skye in the Hebrides.

questions.question: Which unmarried artist finishes her painting on the lawn at the very end of Virginia Woolf's 'To the Lighthouse' (1927), thinking 'I have had my vision'?
questions.explanation: As Mr Ramsay James and Cam finally land at the lighthouse Lily Briscoe draws a single line down the center of her canvas completing her painting.

questions.question: In E. M. Forster's 'A Passage to India' (1924), which young Indian Muslim physician in Chandrapore is put on trial after Adela Quested accuses him of assault in the Marabar Caves?
questions.explanation: Dr Aziz befriends Mrs Moore and Cyril Fielding before Adela Quested hallucinated accusation in the Marabar Caves shatters Anglo-Indian relations.

questions.question: Which 1928 comic first novel by Evelyn Waugh follows the innocent theology student Paul Pennyfeather after he is unjustly expelled from Scone College, Oxford?
questions.explanation: Subtitled An Illustrated Novelette Waugh 1928 debut Decline and Fall sends Paul Pennyfeather to Dr Fagan Welsh school Llanabba Castle.

questions.question: Which popular 1929 picaresque novel by J. B. Priestley brings together the Yorkshire joiner Jess Oakroyd, Inigo Jollifant, and Miss Elizabeth Trant to form a concert troupe?
questions.explanation: Priestley 1929 bestseller The Good Companions won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and celebrated resilient provincial characters.

questions.question: Which 1934 historical novel by Robert Graves is written as the secret autobiography of a stuttering, limping Roman emperor who survives the intrigues of Livia and Caligula?
questions.explanation: Drawing on Tacitus Suetonius and Cassius Dio Robert Graves published I Claudius and its sequel Claudius the God in 1934.

questions.question: In the subtitle of his 1919 play 'Heartbreak House', depicting cultured Europe drifting toward World War I in Captain Shotover's house, Bernard Shaw called it 'A Fantasia in the ______ Manner':
questions.explanation: Inspired by the plays of Anton Chekhov Shaw subtitled Heartbreak House A Fantasia in the Russian Manner on English Themes.

questions.question: Which 1923 chronicle play by George Bernard Shaw dramatizes the rise, heresy trial at Rouen, and 1920 canonization of the Maid of Orléans?
questions.explanation: Written shortly after Joan of Arc 1920 canonization Shaw Saint Joan premiered in December 1923 and led directly to his 1925 Nobel Prize.

questions.question: Which 1935 debut novel by Mulk Raj Anand, published in London with a preface by E. M. Forster, chronicles a single day in the life of the young sweeper Bakha?
questions.explanation: Rejected by nineteen publishers before Wishart Books issued it in 1935 with E M Forster preface Untouchable launched Mulk Raj Anand career.

questions.question: Which 1935 debut novel by R. K. Narayan, championed by Graham Greene, introduced the fictional South Indian town of Malgudi?
questions.explanation: Graham Greene recommended Narayan manuscript to Hamish Hamilton who published Swami and Friends in October 1935.

questions.question: Which two iconic figures of the British Empire and its literature died within two days of each other in January 1936?
options: Rudyard Kipling and King George V
W. B. Yeats and King George VI
Thomas Hardy and King Edward VII
questions.explanation: Rudyard Kipling died on 18 January 1936 and his close friend King George V died two days later on 20 January 1936.
